character_and_relationship_context: Ciarán Walsh has lived in the same small stone house on the edge of Galway for eight years. The salt wind has bleached the limewash to pale grey. The house has one bedroom, a kitchen that smells of diesel and solder, and a back shed workbench where he rewinds alternators and replaces shackles. He works remotely for a Dublin software firm, his mornings spent in a tidy kitchen corner with a laptop propped on a stack of old sailing manuals. His colleagues know him only as the efficient voice on the line who never turns on his camera. When a build fails, he says little, but within an hour he has pushed a fix that is so cleanly documented that no one thinks to ask for an explanation. He has always been self-contained, methodical, and wary of attention. Growing up in a farming family inland from Galway, he learned early that dependency meant vulnerability. His father was quiet and repaired his own machinery, saying little at the dinner table. When Ciarán was fifteen, a summer storm collapsed a cattle shed, and the family spent a week salvaging timber and re-setting the roof without asking neighbours for help. That week hardened something in him: he discovered he could fix almost anything if he studied it carefully, and he preferred to solve his own problems. On weekends he sails his aging twenty-foot sloop alone, sometimes for hours, knowing every bolt, seam, and quirk of the engine. He never races and never joins the marina's social gatherings. He returns at dusk, secures the lines, and walks home without a word. His neighbours expect his politeness—a raised hand, a brief nod—but nothing more. He does not attend local festivals, does not join the church committee, and does not stop for tea when a conversation lingers. Yet every Friday, without fail, he walks to the footbridge at the edge of the tidal marsh and replaces the broken step he noticed the week before. He carries a spare piece of treated oak in his rucksack, cuts it to size with a handsaw kept in the shed, and fits it while the morning mist is still low. No one sees him do it, but the step is always solid. This is the one act of care he permits himself, and it is deliberate: he knows his neighbours use the bridge to reach the shops, and he knows they will never ask him for help. He prefers to give without being asked, to fix what is broken without explanation. His core tension is that he values his independence above all, yet cannot stand to see a small failure go unrepaired. He wants to be left alone, but he also wants to matter. The footbridge step is his compromise—a quiet proof that he is capable of kindness, so long as no one makes him speak it aloud. The years alone have not hardened him so much as sharpened his sense of what he owes his place. He is comfortable, with savings and a boat that needs new rigging, but he has no intention of buying it. He is settled in a way that suggests he has made peace with solitude, though a stranger might notice how his eyes follow a child crossing the bridge, or how he lingers longer than necessary when the harbour lights come on. Aoife is his only sibling, eight years younger, living inland near Tuam; their contact is a few short calls a year, mostly initiated by her. He helped her fit kitchen units two summers ago and left before tea was poured, as she expected. She knows he prefers solitude and never pushes, but she checks in when she is nearby. When he gets an unexpected family call mid-job, he usually lets it ring and calls back later the same evening. On the rare occasions he agrees to meet someone, he arrives early and keeps the conversation brief. He has declined casual neighbour invitations consistently, but he has shown up for practical emergencies.
objective_situation: On Saturday afternoon, Ciarán is in the shed re-winding an alternator when his phone buzzes. It is his younger sister, Aoife, who rarely calls. She says she is driving back from a work trip and is passing through Galway, but she is already at the petrol station near the footbridge. She has forty minutes before she needs to head inland to collect her kids from school. She asks if he can meet her there for a coffee. He can see the station roof from his garden, but he is in the middle of a delicate solder job and has not showered since morning.
state_and_available_memories: At the time of the call, Ciarán is kneeling on the shed floor, reheating a solder joint with steady, slightly tacky hands. He has not eaten since breakfast, his hair is flattened with sweat, and the alternator is half-wound. He had planned to finish this winding, then walk to the footbridge to re-check the step he replaced last Friday. The familiar ring of Aoife's number brings back the memory of her last call, which was to tell him about the children's school play. Looking toward the station roof, he remembers the Tuesday he saw her car parked there and assumed she was just filling up, only to learn later she had waited an hour hoping he would come out.
name: Ciarán Walsh
